items.prompt: What is the sense of smell also called?

options.label: Olfaction
options.feedback: That's right. The sense of smell is known as olfaction.

options.label: Gustation
options.feedback: Gustation is the sense of taste, not smell.

options.label: Audition
options.feedback: Audition is the sense of hearing.

options.label: Somatosensation
options.feedback: Somatosensation covers touch, pressure, and pain, not smell.

items.exp_text: The sense of smell is called olfaction. It is one of the special senses, and it lets the body perceive odors.

items.prompt: Where in the body does the sense of smell begin?

options.label: In the mouth
options.feedback: The mouth is involved with taste, not the start of smell. Smell begins in the nasal cavity.

options.label: In the nasal cavity
options.feedback: Yes. An odor binds to a receptor inside the nasal cavity to start the sense of smell.

options.label: In the throat
options.feedback: The throat is a passage for air and food, but smell starts higher up in the nose.

options.label: In the ear
options.feedback: The ear handles hearing and balance, not the beginning of smell.

items.ko_line: That location does not detect odors.
items.exp_text: Smell begins when an odor molecule binds to a receptor in the nasal cavity. That binding sends a signal along the olfactory system to the brain.

items.prompt: What happens when an odor binds to a receptor in the nose?

options.label: The odor is dissolved and destroyed
options.feedback: Binding does not destroy the molecule; it starts a nerve signal instead.

options.label: The odor is stored in the receptor
options.feedback: Receptors do not store odors. They trigger a signal that travels onward.

options.label: A signal is sent through the olfactory system
options.feedback: Correct. The binding transmits a signal from the receptor through the olfactory system toward the brain.

options.label: The receptor multiplies
options.feedback: Receptors do not multiply from a single odor binding; a signal is sent.

items.ko_line: Binding does not store or destroy.
items.exp_text: When an odor binds to a receptor in the nasal cavity, it transmits a signal through the olfactory system. That signal eventually reaches the brain for identification.

items.prompt: What do the glomeruli do in the olfactory system?

options.label: They produce mucus
options.feedback: Mucus is not made by glomeruli; glomeruli collect signals from receptors.

options.label: They filter out odors
options.feedback: Glomeruli do not filter; they aggregate signals from many receptors.

options.label: They create odor molecules
options.feedback: Odor molecules come from outside, not from glomeruli.

options.label: They aggregate signals from receptors
options.feedback: Yes. Glomeruli combine signals from many receptors and pass them to the olfactory bulb.

items.ko_line: That is not what glomeruli do.
items.exp_text: Glomeruli gather signals from multiple olfactory receptors and send them onward to the olfactory bulb. From there, the input connects with parts of the brain handling smell, memory, and emotion.

items.prompt: Which of these can interfere with a normal sense of smell?

options.label: Damage to the nose or smell receptors
options.feedback: Correct. Damage to the nose or smell receptors is one of the listed causes of a disrupted sense of smell.

options.label: Wearing glasses
options.feedback: Glasses sit on the face and do not interfere with smell receptors or the nose's function.

options.label: Listening to loud sounds
options.feedback: Loud sounds affect hearing, not the sense of smell.

options.label: Eating spicy food
options.feedback: Spicy food can cause a burning feeling, but it does not interfere with the sense of smell itself.

items.exp_text: Several things can disrupt normal smell, including damage to the nose or smell receptors, anosmia, nasal congestion, upper respiratory infections, traumatic brain injury, and neurodegenerative disease.

options.label: An inability to taste
options.feedback: Taste loss is a different condition, not anosmia.

options.label: An inability to hear
options.feedback: Hearing loss is not anosmia.

options.label: An inability to smell
options.feedback: Yes. Anosmia is the loss or absence of the sense of smell.

options.label: An inability to feel touch
options.feedback: Loss of touch sensation is not anosmia.

items.ko_line: That is a different sensory loss.
items.exp_text: Anosmia is the inability to smell. It is listed as one of the things that can interfere with a normal sense of smell.

items.prompt: What does the olfactory bulb connect with after receiving signals?

options.label: The spinal cord only
options.feedback: The olfactory bulb connects with brain regions, not the spinal cord.

options.label: Parts of the brain that handle smell, memory, and emotion
options.feedback: Correct. The olfactory bulb starts interacting with brain areas for smell identification, memory, and emotion.

options.label: The muscles of the nose
options.feedback: Muscles are not the target of olfactory signals; brain regions are.

options.label: The ears directly
options.feedback: The olfactory bulb does not connect to the ears. It interacts with the brain.

items.ko_line: That is not where the bulb connects.
items.exp_text: After glomeruli pass signals to the olfactory bulb, that input starts interacting with brain regions responsible for identifying smells, remembering them, and linking to emotions.

items.prompt: What is the role of smell in flavor perception?

options.label: Smell has no role in flavor
options.feedback: Smell does play a role; retronasal smell is the biggest contributor to flavor sensation.

options.label: Smell only works during swallowing
options.feedback: Flavor from smell occurs during exhalation, not swallowing.

options.label: Smell only works during inhalation
options.feedback: Proper smell happens during inhalation, but the smell's contribution to flavor occurs during exhalation.

options.label: Retronasal smell plays the biggest role
options.feedback: Yes. Retronasal smell is the largest contributor to the sensation of flavor.

items.exp_text: Flavor comes from combining several senses, and retronasal smell is the biggest part. During chewing, odorants enter the nasal cavity on exhalation, and the brain treats that smell as coming from the mouth.

items.prompt: What is unusual about the olfactory system compared with other human senses?

options.label: It bypasses the thalamus and connects directly to the forebrain
options.feedback: Correct. The olfactory system is the only human sense that skips the thalamus and goes straight to the forebrain.

options.label: It connects to the spinal cord first
options.feedback: The olfactory system does not go through the spinal cord.

options.label: It does not send signals to the brain
options.feedback: It absolutely sends signals to the brain; it bypasses the thalamus but still reaches the forebrain.

options.label: It uses the same path as hearing
options.feedback: Hearing goes through the thalamus, unlike smell.

items.ko_line: That is not how smell works.
items.exp_text: The olfactory system is the only human sense that bypasses the thalamus and connects directly to the forebrain. All other senses relay through the thalamus before reaching higher brain areas.
